paragraphs: Sovereignty is indivisible for the same reason that it is inalienable. For a will either is general or it is not;[1] it is either the will of the whole body of the people, or only of a part of it. In the first case, the will, once declared, is an act of Sovereignty and makes law. In the second, it is merely a particular will, or an act of magistracy — at most a decree.

But our political theorists, unable to divide Sovereignty in principle, divide it according to its object. They split it into force and will, into legislative power and executive power, into the rights of taxation, justice and war, and into internal administration and the power to make treaties with other nations. Sometimes they confuse all these sections, and sometimes they distinguish them. They turn the Sovereign into a fantastic being put together from several connected pieces. It is as if they were making a man out of several bodies, one with eyes, one with arms, another with feet, and each with nothing else. We are told that the jugglers of Japan dismember a child before the eyes of the spectators, then throw all the limbs into the air one after another, and the child falls down alive and whole. The conjuring tricks of our political theorists are very much like that. First they dismember the body politic by an illusion worthy of a fairground, and then they join it together again, we do not know how.

This error comes from a lack of exact notions about Sovereign authority, and from taking for parts of it what are only emanations from it. For example, the acts of declaring war and making peace have been regarded as acts of Sovereignty. But they are not, since these acts do not make law. They are only the application of a law, a particular act that decides how the law applies, as we shall see clearly once the idea attached to the word _law_ has been defined.

If we examined the other divisions in the same way, we should find that whenever Sovereignty seems to be divided, there is an illusion. The rights that are taken to be parts of Sovereignty are really all subordinate to it, and always presuppose supreme wills of which they only carry out the decisions.

It is impossible to measure how much obscurity this lack of exactness has thrown over the judgments of writers on political right, when they have used the principles they laid down to decide the respective rights of kings and peoples. Anyone can see, in Chapters III and IV of the First Book of Grotius, how that learned man and his translator Barbeyrac entangle and tie themselves up in their own sophistries, for fear of saying too little or too much of what they think, and so offending the interests they have to keep on good terms with. Grotius, a refugee in France, discontented with his own country and eager to win the favor of Louis XIII, to whom his book is dedicated, spares no effort to rob the peoples of all their rights and invest kings with them by every conceivable artifice. This would also have suited Barbeyrac, who dedicated his translation to George I of England. But unfortunately the expulsion of James II, which he called an “abdication,” forced him to be wary, to shuffle and to equivocate, in order to avoid making William out to be a usurper. If these two writers had adopted the true principles, all difficulties would have been removed and they would always have been consistent. But it would have been a sad truth for them to tell, and would have won them the favor of no one except the people. Besides, truth is no road to fortune, and the people hand out neither ambassadorships, nor professorships, nor pensions.
